content: Abstract Background: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remains a major clinical and pathological concern in India. Its presentation varies by anatomical site and histological pattern, and recognizing uncommon variants, along with the appropriate interpretation of p16 expression, may provide useful diagnostic information. Objective: This study aimed to describe the demographic and clinicopathological profile of 1,000 HNSCC cases, with particular attention to histological variants, cervical lymph node involvement, and p16 expression. Materials and methods: This retrospective observational study included 1,000 histologically confirmed HNSCC cases diagnosed at a tertiary-care teaching hospital between January 2023 and December 2024. Age, sex, tumor site, histological grade, nodal status, histological variants, recurrence, and second primary malignancies were reviewed. p16 immunohistochemistry was performed in 109 cases with suitable tissue, including 50 conventional SCCs and 59 histological variants. Strong, diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in more than 70% of tumor cells was considered positive. Results: The cohort included 832 men and 168 women, with most patients aged 51-70 years. The oral tongue was the most frequent individual site (24.7%), while supraglottic and glottic tumors together accounted for 29.4% of cases. Well-differentiated SCC was the predominant grade (71.0%). Cervical lymph node metastasis was present in 147 patients (14.7%), with the highest within-grade frequency in moderately differentiated SCC (20.4%); the association between histological grade and nodal metastasis was significant (χ2 = 9.89, p = 0.007). Of the 59 histological variants, 32 (54.2%) were p16 positive, with papillary SCC accounting for most positive cases. Of the 50 conventional SCCs, 20 (40.0%) showed p16 positivity. Twenty-five patients had second primary malignancies, and 16 had recurrence. Conclusions: This large single-center series demonstrates the clinicopathological diversity of HNSCC in an Indian tertiary-care setting. Histological variant recognition and assessment of nodal involvement remain important components of pathological evaluation. p16 immunohistochemistry may provide useful supplementary information in selected cases, but its expression should be interpreted as a surrogate marker rather than definitive evidence of HPV-driven disease without molecular confirmation. Introduction Head and neck cancers remain an important cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide. According to GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates from the International Agency for Research on Cancer, cancers of the lip and oral cavity accounted for 389,846 new cases and 188,438 deaths globally. During the same period, laryngeal cancer accounted for 189,191 new cases and 103,359 deaths, while approximately 120,434 cases of nasopharyngeal cancer and 86,257 cases of hypopharyngeal cancer were reported worldwide [1]. The burden is particularly relevant to India, where lip and oral cavity cancer was the most frequently diagnosed cancer among men in 2022, with an estimated 107,812 new cases [1]. More than 90% of malignant tumors arising from the mucosal surfaces of the oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx are squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) [2]. Despite improvements in surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic treatment, late presentation, locoregional recurrence, and second primary malignancies continue to influence the clinical course of head and neck SCC (HNSCC) [3]. The distribution and etiological profile of HNSCC vary considerably across geographical regions. In South and Southeast Asia, including India, tobacco smoking, smokeless tobacco, use of areca nut and betel quid, and alcohol consumption are well-established contributors to the high burden of oral and other head and neck cancers [4,5]. These exposures are particularly relevant as background epidemiological factors in the Indian population, although they were not the primary focus of the present clinicopathological analysis. In contrast, the incidence of HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC has increased substantially in several Western populations, with HPV-16 accounting for most HPV-driven tumors at this site [6]. HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma is now recognized as a biologically distinct disease with differences in treatment response and prognosis compared with conventional tobacco-related HNSCC [7]. Clinical presentation varies by anatomical site and disease extent. Patients may present with a persistent oral ulcer, dysphagia, change in voice, throat discomfort, or cervical lymphadenopathy, and some tumors are first diagnosed at an advanced stage [8]. Histopathological examination therefore remains central to diagnosis and tumor characterization. Although conventional SCC forms the largest group, HNSCC includes several less common histological variants with distinctive microscopic appearances and, in some instances, different biological behavior and prognostic implications [9]. Correct recognition of these variants is consequently important during routine pathological evaluation. Assessment of HPV-related disease has also become increasingly relevant, particularly in oropharyngeal SCC. p16 immunohistochemistry is widely used as a practical surrogate marker of HPV-associated carcinogenesis; however, p16 overexpression does not by itself establish the presence of transcriptionally active HPV, especially in tumors arising outside the oropharynx. Its findings should therefore be interpreted together with tumor site, morphology, and, where clinically required, HPV-specific molecular testing [10]. This distinction is particularly important when examining p16 expression across different anatomical sites and uncommon histological variants. Large single-center series describing the clinicopathological spectrum of HNSCC, including histological variants and p16 findings, remain relatively limited in India. This study aimed to describe the demographic and clinicopathological spectrum of 1,000 HNSCC cases, with particular attention to histological variants and p16 expression. Materials & Methods Study design and setting This retrospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Pathology, Government ENT Hospital, Osmania Medical College, Hyderabad, India. The study included patients with histologically confirmed HNSCC diagnosed between January 2023 and December 2024. The unit of analysis was the individual patient with histologically confirmed HNSCC. The study primarily described the demographic and clinicopathological profile of HNSCC, with additional evaluation of histological variants, cervical lymph node involvement, and p16 immunohistochemical expression. Ethical approval The Institutional Ethics Committee and Biomedical and Health Research Committee of Osmania Medical College approved the study protocol (approval number: IEC/OMC/M.NO (18)/P-192, dated June 8, 2026). As this was a retrospective study, the analysis was based on previously diagnosed cases, existing clinical records, pathology reports, and archived pathological material. The study required no additional investigations, treatment procedures, specimen collection, or direct patient contact. All identifying information was removed before analysis, and patient confidentiality was maintained throughout. In accordance with the approved retrospective study protocol, separate study-specific informed consent was not applicable. Case identification and eligibility criteria A census-based sampling approach was used rather than calculating a predetermined sample size. All consecutive histologically confirmed HNSCC cases diagnosed during the two-year study period were screened for eligibility. A total of 1,000 cases satisfying the study criteria were included in the final analysis. Eligible cases comprised primary SCCs arising from the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, and other included mucosal head and neck sites. Cases were excluded when the available material was inadequate for histopathological assessment, paraffin blocks were poorly preserved, or essential clinical or pathological information required for the analysis was unavailable. Each patient was assigned to one primary anatomical site for analysis. Recurrent tumors and second primary malignancies were identified from the available clinical and pathology records and recorded separately. These events were described as additional clinical outcomes and were not counted as new independent primary cases within the principal 1,000-case analysis. Data collection and variable definitions Clinical and pathological information was retrieved from hospital case records, pathology requisition forms, archived histopathology reports, and available laboratory records. Variables included age, sex, primary anatomical site, histological grade, histological variant, cervical lymph node status, recurrence, second primary malignancy, and p16 immunohistochemical expression when tested. Age was grouped into predefined categories for descriptive analysis. Anatomical sites were coded as mutually exclusive categories so that each patient contributed to only one primary-site group. Histological grade was classified as well differentiated, moderately differentiated, or poorly differentiated. For the principal statistical analysis, cervical lymph node status was recorded from available clinical and pathological documentation as either nodal involvement present or absent. Some records included information on tobacco use, smokeless tobacco, alcohol consumption, areca nut, and related exposures, but these data were not recorded consistently across the cohort. Reliable definitions of duration, dose, frequency, and combined exposure could therefore not be applied consistently. Consequently, we excluded risk-factor variables from the quantitative analysis rather than treating them as complete exposure data. Cases with missing information for variables essential to inclusion were excluded during case selection. For variables available only in defined subsets, such as p16 immunohistochemistry, analyses were restricted to cases with recorded results. No statistical imputation of missing values was performed. Histopathological review and analysis Archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue blocks and corresponding histological sections were reviewed. Sections of approximately 3-5 μm thickness were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and examined by light microscopy. Conventional SCC was diagnosed on the basis of standard squamous differentiation and was categorized as well differentiated, moderately differentiated, or poorly differentiated according to established histomorphological criteria. Tumors were also reviewed for recognized histological variants using the applicable World Health Organization classification criteria for head and neck tumors. The histological variants in this series included papillary SCC, verrucous carcinoma, basaloid SCC, spindle cell/sarcomatoid carcinoma, acantholytic SCC, non-keratinizing SCC, and non-keratinizing undifferentiated carcinoma of nasopharyngeal type. Variant classification was based on the characteristic microscopic architecture and cytomorphological features identified on H&E-stained sections. Ascertainment of cervical lymph node status Cervical lymph node involvement was determined from the clinical and pathological information available in the medical record and pathology documentation. For the principal analysis examining the relationship between histological grade and nodal spread, lymph node metastasis was coded as a binary outcome: present or absent. When information on the side or distribution of nodal involvement was available, we retained these findings for descriptive assessment. Selection of cases for p16 immunohistochemistry p16 immunohistochemistry was performed in a defined subset of 109 cases from the main 1,000-case cohort. This group comprised 59 histological variant cases and 50 conventional SCC cases. The 109 cases were not selected because they were already known to be p16-positive, nor were they randomly sampled from the entire cohort. Selection was based on histological morphology and the availability of adequate, well-preserved formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue suitable for immunohistochemical staining. Histological variant cases were included when sufficient tissue was available for p16 assessment. The conventional SCC subset included 40 well-differentiated, eight moderately differentiated, and two poorly differentiated tumors selected from archived cases with suitable tissue. The remaining cases in the overall cohort were not tested because p16 immunohistochemistry was not routinely performed in every HNSCC case during the study period, and appropriate archived tissue was not uniformly available. The p16-tested group should therefore be regarded as an availability-based pathological subset rather than a random or population-representative sample. p16 immunohistochemistry Immunohistochemical staining for p16 was performed on selected formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections using a commercially available monoclonal antibody against p16 (Biogenex) and an avidin-biotin-based detection method. Appropriate positive and negative controls were included with each staining run. Stained sections were evaluated for both nuclear and cytoplasmic immunoreactivity. A case was considered p16 positive when strong, diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic staining involved more than 70% of tumor cells. Cases showing absent, focal, weak, or patchy staining below this threshold were classified as negative. Because HPV-specific molecular testing, such as HPV DNA testing, RNA in situ hybridization, or E6/E7 mRNA analysis, was not performed, p16 immunoreactivity was interpreted as a surrogate marker rather than direct confirmation of HPV-driven carcinogenesis. This distinction was particularly relevant for tumors arising outside the oropharynx. Statistical analysis Data were entered into Excel (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, USA) and analyzed using SPSS Statistics version 25.0 (IBM Corp. Released 2017. IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 25.0. Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics were used for the principal clinicopathological variables. Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages, while age was presented using predefined age categories. Associations between categorical variables were assessed using the Pearson chi-square test when expected cell frequencies were adequate. Fisher’s exact test was used when sparse cell counts made the chi-square approximation inappropriate. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. For the analysis of histological grade and cervical lymph node metastasis, lymph node metastasis was defined as the outcome variable, while histological grade was the exposure variable. Well-differentiated SCC served as the reference category. Unadjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated for comparisons involving moderately differentiated and poorly differentiated SCC. No multivariable regression model was performed. Results Age and sex distribution Among the 1,000 patients with HNSCC, 832 were men and 168 were women, giving a male-to-female ratio of approximately 4.9:1. The largest proportion of patients was in the 51-60-year age group (29.0%), followed by 61-70 years (22.6%) and 41-50 years (22.0%). Patients aged 31-40 years accounted for 14.0% of the cohort, while 6.0% were aged 21-30 years and 6.4% were older than 70 years. Overall, most cases occurred between 41 and 70 years of age, with a clear male predominance across the age groups. Anatomical site distribution Table 1 shows the anatomical distribution of the 1,000 HNSCC cases. The oral tongue was the most frequently involved individual site, accounting for 247 cases (24.7%). This was followed by the supraglottis (162 cases; 16.2%), buccal mucosa (159 cases; 15.9%), and glottis (132 cases; 13.2%). Hypopharyngeal tumors accounted for 110 cases (11.0%). Less frequently involved sites were the alveolus/gingiva (6.4%), oropharynx (5.9%), floor of mouth (3.5%), and nasopharynx (3.2%). When grouped by region, oral cavity tumors formed the largest category, while supraglottic and glottic tumors together represented 29.4% of the cohort. Histological grade and cervical lymph node metastasis Of the 1,000 HNSCC cases, 710 (71.0%) were well differentiated, 245 (24.5%) were moderately differentiated, and 45 (4.5%) were poorly differentiated. Cervical lymph node metastasis was identified in 147 patients, corresponding to an overall nodal metastasis rate of 14.7%. The proportion of patients with nodal metastasis differed significantly across histological grades (χ2 = 9.89, df = 2, p = 0.007). Lymph node involvement was present in 94 of 710 well-differentiated tumors (13.2%), 50 of 245 moderately differentiated tumors (20.4%), and three of 45 poorly differentiated tumors (6.7%). Using well-differentiated SCC as the reference category, moderately differentiated SCC was associated with higher odds of cervical lymph node metastasis (OR = 1.68, 95% CI 1.15-2.45; p = 0.007). Poorly differentiated SCC showed lower observed odds of nodal involvement (OR = 0.47, 95% CI 0.14-1.54), but this difference was not statistically significant (Fisher’s exact p = 0.255) (Table 2). The finding in the poorly differentiated group should be interpreted cautiously because only three patients in this category had nodal metastasis. p16 expression in 59 histological variant cases A total of 59 histological variant cases were evaluated by p16 immunohistochemistry. Of these, 32 (54.2%) were p16 positive and 27 (45.8%) were negative. Papillary SCC was the largest subgroup, comprising 32 cases, of which 28 (87.5%) showed p16 positivity. content: Your Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More Video Events Specialties Topics RegisterLog In Medscape Medical NewsMedBrief Medbrief Reduced-Dose Radiation Cuts Patient-Reported Toxicity in HPV-Related Oropharyngeal Cancer October 05, 2026 0 TOPLINE Among patients with human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) who had a complete response to induction chemotherapy, those who received reduced-dose intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) reported significantly less difficulty swallowing and less voice impairment than those who received standard-dose IMRT, per the phase 2 E1308 trial. Disease-specific patient-reported outcome (PRO) tools detected these differences more reliably than general quality-of-life measures. A historical comparison with the earlier E2399 trial supported similar reductions in toxicity with IMRT vs three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy (3DRT). METHODOLOGY A phase 2 trial, E2399, showed that HPV-positive oropharynx cancer responds well to chemoradiation, raising the possibility of reducing treatment intensity without compromising cure rates. Because high-dose radiation drives most acute and long-term toxicity, the follow-up E1308 trial tested whether a response to induction chemotherapy could guide the use of lower-dose IMRT. This prospective phase 2 trial (ECOG-ACRIN E1308) evaluated reduced-dose IMRT of 54 Gy against standard-dose IMRT of 69.3 Gy in patients with HPV-associated OPSCC who achieved a complete clinical response to induction chemotherapy. A total of 80 patients were treated in E1308; 62 of 80 (78%) achieved a complete response to induction chemotherapy with paclitaxel, cisplatin, and cetuximab and received 54 Gy, while the remainder received 69.3 Gy. Fifty-one patients who remained progression-free at 12 months (42 patients who received 54 Gy and nine patients who received 69.3 Gy) were evaluated for PROs. Researchers assessed disease-specific symptom burden using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Head & Neck (FACT-HN) and the Vanderbilt Head and Neck Symptom Survey Version 2 (VHNSSv2) and general quality of life using the Katz Index of Independence in Activities of Daily Living (ADL), Brief Fatigue Index (BFI), Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL), Baecke physical activity scale, and Community Health Activities Model Program for Seniors (CHAMPS) questionnaire. All measures were administered at baseline and at 6, 12, 24, and 30 months post-treatment. Toxicity outcomes in E1308 were compared historically with those of 69 patients treated in the earlier E2399 trial who received induction chemotherapy followed by 3DRT at 70 Gy over 7 weeks with concurrent weekly paclitaxel. TAKEAWAY At 6 months, VHNSSv2 scores indicated that reduced-dose IMRT eased swallowing of solids (P = .011) and liquids (P = .004), voice impairment (P = .026), dry mouth (P = .02), and neck/shoulder movement limitations (P = .03) compared with standard-dose IMRT. FACT-HN scores indicated that the reduced-dose IMRT group had less difficulty eating solid foods at 6 months (P = .054) and better voice strength and quality (P = .038) than the standard-dose group. Comparing reduced-dose IMRT (54 Gy) in E1308 with 3DRT (70 Gy) in E2399, FACT-HN scores showed that IMRT was associated with better ability to eat solid food at 12 months (P = .0103) and greater ability to eat preferred foods (P = .0067). Additionally, patients who received 3DRT had higher rates of grade ≥ 3 oral mucositis (58% vs 29%; P = .0003), dysphagia (39% vs 15%; P = .001), and esophagitis (8% vs 0%; P = .023) than those who received reduced-dose IMRT. General quality-of-life tools — CHAMPS, Katz ADL, BFI, IADL, and Baecke — did not detect significant reductions in toxicity or differences in function or fatigue between the dose groups. IN PRACTICE "Our data from the first prospective study of radiation dose reduction in treatment responsive HPV-associated oropharynx cancer demonstrate a statistically significantly less worsening of swallowing dysfunction and voice impairment for patients treated with reduced-dose IMRT based on disease-specific VHNSSv2 and FACT-HN instruments at 6 months post-treatment. This supports our initial hypothesis that reducing radiation dose and duration will reduce chronic symptom burden and has spawned a plethora of additional deintensification paradigms in ongoing clinical trials," the authors concluded. SOURCE The study, led by Anthony J. Cmelak, MD, Vanderbilt University/Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville, Tennessee, was published online in JCO Oncology Advances. LIMITATIONS Small standard-dose cohorts and declining PRO completion at later time points limited statistical power. Comparisons were not randomized, with E2399 including both HPV-positive and HPV-negative patients, introducing heterogeneity. Historical 3DRT-vs-IMRT comparisons also reflected inherent technical differences between the two radiation approaches beyond dose alone. DISCLOSURES This study was supported by the ECOG-ACRIN Cancer Research Group and grants from the National Cancer Institute of the National Institutes of Health. Several authors reported consulting, research funding, employment, leadership, or ownership ties to pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, including Merck, AstraZeneca, Regeneron, Takeda, and others. Pregnancy HPV Vaccine May Have Benefits Beyond Cancer Protection You can still access 2 more articles for free. - HPV vaccination may reduce pregnancy complications - Women vaccinated against HPV had lower risks of preterm birth, early rupture of the amniotic sac and having a very small baby - Women vaccinated before age 17 showed stronger benefits THURSDAY, Oct. 8, 2026 (HealthDay News) — The HPV vaccine is best known for protecting against cervical cancer. But, it may have another major benefit: reducing the risk of serious pregnancy complications. A team led by Zhongsong Zhang, of the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, conducted a large study that looked at more than 624,000 first-time births. About 93,000 of the women had been vaccinated against human papillomavirus, HPV — a common, sexually transmitted infection that can cause precancerous and cancerous changes. Those who were vaccinated had lower odds of several complications, including preterm and very preterm birth, the amniotic sac rupturing too early, and having a severely small baby. The link was generally stronger among women vaccinated before age 17. They had about 10% lower odds of preterm birth and 11% lower odds of spontaneous preterm birth. Researchers said vaccination may help by preventing HPV infection and reducing the need for procedures to remove abnormal cervical tissue. These procedures have been linked to a higher risk of preterm birth. Because this was an observational study, it can't prove cause and effect. But researchers say the study's large size, high-quality data and long follow-up strengthen the findings. "Our results suggest that human papillomavirus vaccination is not only safe with respect to pregnancy outcomes but may also confer additional benefits by reducing the risk of adverse events," they said in a news release. The findings were published Oct. 7 in The BMJ. More information The Cleveland Clinic has more on the human papillomavirus. content: Advertising Volume 55, Issue 10, October 2026 Cancer screening in LGBTQIA+ populations Matthew J Ruhl Background Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer/questioning, intersex and asexual/aromantic (LGBTQIA+, the plus referring to other sexuality and gender diverse groups) peoples in Australia experience lower levels of cancer screening and preventive activities when compared with the general population. This is especially the case for transgender and gender diverse (TGD) peoples, who experience additional barriers to access and discrimination above the rest of LGBTQIA+ peoples. Objective This article seeks to enhance cancer screening engagement among LGBTQIA+ individuals by addressing underscreening within these populations and offering strategies for improvement within primary care, including specific examples relevant to TGD peoples. Discussion Enhanced, individualised patient assessment, education and practitioner recommendations for cancer screening and prevention – supported by practitioner upskilling, LGBTQIA+ inclusivity training and the development of safer healthcare environments – may increase participation in screening programs, ultimately leading to earlier detection and better cancer outcomes. Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer/questioning, intersex, asexual/aromantic and other sexuality and gender diverse (LGBTQIA+) populations (noting some peoples are not well included in the literature and may not feel well aligned with the acronym, such as intersex peoples) experience healthcare differently to the wider population, with heteronormativity, minority stress, discrimination, uncertainties in finding safe spaces and practitioners, and other systemic and individual barriers, all influenced by intersectionality.1,2 Intersectionality is a term coined to describe the multiple overlapping and multiplying oppressions faced by many individuals,3 which might, for example, include gender, sexuality, ethnicity, disability and so on, and may further contribute to screening barriers. For transgender and gender diverse (TGD) peoples, there is insufficient evidence as yet to determine the effect of gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT) on long-term cancer risks.4–6 Many guidelines, including those regarding cancer screening and prevention, are based on large population studies that either do not include or do not acknowledge LGBTQIA+ individuals, making clear guidance for these peoples difficult.6 Many cancer registries do not specifically consider TGD peoples, which also limits their applicability.7 As a result, most guidance is extrapolated on the basis of known risk factors and, for TGD peoples, which organs or tissues they possess.5,6 Uptake of cancer screening is influenced by practitioner recommendation;8 this is specifically seen in TGD patients.9 Consideration of individual patient barriers, including patient education and test acceptability, may improve uptake. Some discomforts may be negotiated by prior preparation (eg cervical screening in transgender people with a cervix, discussed below) or prior communication (eg a call or letter to a provider), potentially improving the likelihood of patient engagement. Aim This paper aims to provide an overview of LGBTQIA+ populations’ engagement with, and uptake of, current cancer screening programs in Australia, with discussion of screening programs and what this means for TGD patients, including barriers to screening, and practice modifications to improve screening. Overarching principles Recognising each patient as an individual when determining appropriate preventive and screening activities is essential. This is also the foundation to building rapport, delivering tailored education, promoting positive healthcare behaviours and addressing potential barriers to accessing healthcare. LGBTQIA+-specific educational materials should be provided, where available.10 Use of appropriate and preferred anatomical terms for individual patients is also recommended, such as chest tissue rather than breast tissue.10,11 Practitioner flexibility, to adapt and work collaboratively with each patient, is therefore ideal. Organ- and tissue-specific screening is currently recommended; for example, if a patient has a cervix, then application of population-based screening recommendations for cervical cancer should be recommended.5 Some risk factors may influence additional specific screening or cancer vigilance, such as medication and meningiomas.12 Table 1 briefly summarises the recommendations for LGBTQIA+ cancer screening. National cancer screening programs Australia has four national screening programs, as follows.13–16 Breast cancer Breast cancer affects TGD peoples less often than cisgender females but more often than cisgender males, potentially because of TGD peoples’ lower lifetime exposure to oestrogen and progesterone when compared with cisgender females.6,17,18 Of people aged 50–74 years who live in Victoria and are eligible for breast screening, 22.6% of LGBTQI+ peoples have never had a mammogram, compared with 10.4% of the non-LGBTQI+ population.19 It was found that 60% of transgender women, 52% of transgender men and 42% of gender diverse people had ‘little concern’ for developing breast cancer, which may indicate a need for increased patient education.20 Other international breast screen programs, such as in Canada, show lower screening rates for TGD peoples than for the general population.21 Many patients will be happy to engage with screening; hence, it should not be assumed there is a barrier. Clinician recommendation and/or a reminder may be all that is needed. Screening recommendations should consider age at which GAHT was commenced, duration of GAHT and whether the patient has had ‘top surgery’ (such as mastectomy, acknowledging ‘mastectomy’ is a term rarely used in the TGD community), though broadly, cisgender recommendations for screening apply.17,18 State-based guidance is described in Table 2. Screening via private referral is also possible if required. Patients should be counselled that they may be questioned about their GAHT as it increases breast tissue density, which may make interpretation difficult.17 Cervical cancer Only 38.9% of eligible TGD peoples in Australia have been screened for cervical cancer.22 Many transgender men have never had a cervical screening test (CST),20,23 and nearly 9 out of 20 TGD people with a cervix have never had a CST recommended by a health professional.23 Dysphoria from CST collection may be a significant barrier for some patients,23 though many patients will be comfortable to proceed and may simply benefit from a routine reminder. The human papillomavirus (HPV) is the causative agent for most cervical cancer within LGBTQIA+ populations as for within the broader population.17,24 HPV vaccination should be encouraged within the usual schedule on the National Immunisation Program, or recommended if not previously accessed,18 and CST offered per the National Cervical Screening Program Guideline (the Guideline).15 The Guideline comments on some of the barriers to a CST and recommends asking patients about anatomy terms (eg some patients may prefer terms other than vagina and cervix, such as front hole, though many will find anatomical terms acceptable) and includes a link to letter templates that describe many of the techniques that can be considered to increase patient comfort during a CST.15 A fact sheet is also available.25 Topics include self-collection (where appropriate), self-insertion of the speculum and use of the smallest speculum, and patient preferences regarding positioning, environment and discussion during the test.15 The Guideline also guides clinicians to further national information and resources on engaging LGBTQI+ peoples in cervical screening.26 Given the test can be physically uncomfortable because of atrophy, patients presumed female at birth (PFAB) taking masculinising GAHT may be offered intravaginal oestrogen beforehand if needed, which decreases the discomfort from atrophy and increases result quality, similar to postmenopausal cisgender women.27 Not all patients will require this, especially if self-collecting, but suitable options include an oestradiol 10 microgram pessary or an application of estriol 0.1% cream daily for 2 weeks prior to the test, ceasing 1–2 days beforehand.15 Bowel cancer The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (NBCSP) shows low levels of engagement across the entire population; only 40% of the eligible 6 million people invited to participate between January 2021 and December 2022 returned their envelopes.16 LGBTQ+ engagement is mostly unknown, though a 2017 Victorian survey found similar engagement levels to the non-LGBTQ+ population.19 The prevalence of colorectal cancer is not known to be different between LGBTQIA+ peoples and the rest of the population (except possibly for anal cancers12), so screening should be recommended for all LGBTQIA+ peoples per the program guidelines.6 Anal cancer Men who have sex with men (MSM) and who are also living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) have approximately 60 times the rate of anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) when compared with the general population. High-risk HPV (HRHPV) is detected in 88% of ASCC.28 In Australia, the availability of high-resolution anoscopy (HRA) is currently extremely limited. For at-risk individuals who do not have access to HRA, the Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine (ASHM) recommends that anal swabs for HPV and cytology should not be collected. Instead, it is recommended that there be annual assessment of history and symptoms, an annual digital anorectal examination (DARE) and annual examination of the peri-anal region.28 The screening recommendations apply to people living with HIV aged 18 years and over.28 Lung cancer Recently implemented, the National Lung Cancer Screening Program includes screening by a practitioner-referred low-dose computed tomography (CT) scan on the basis of age and smoking history.14 With higher smoking rates in Australian LGBT populations,29 screening should be recommended where appropriate, especially given this program is more practitioner directed than the other three. Cancer surveillance Neither prostate cancer nor skin cancer have a program of coordinated screening, though both are common, and the discussion of screening and surveillance is recommended. They are discussed here to provide support for patient education. Prostate With multiple possible symptoms (and asymptomatic presentation), and some challenges in using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) as a screening test, screening for prostate cancer among cisgender men is considered on a case-by-case basis after a thorough discussion of the relative risks and benefits.30 TGD people with prostate glands typically retain their prostate glands even following gender affirmative surgery (which many transgender people choose not to access, or are unable to access).31 If DARE is subsequently required, noting that this is no longer a recommended part of prostate cancer screening, the prostate gland may sometimes be palpable only via their neovagina.31 Feminising GAHT lowers the risk of prostate cancer,6,32,33 as anti-androgens used in GAHT may also be used in treating prostate cancer.34 Feminising GAHT can also lead to a marked reduction in PSA, which can make interpretation of PSA results difficult.31,35 TGD peoples with prostate glands who are not using GAHT have a risk of prostate cancer similar to cisgender counterparts.31 Counselling and the offer of PSA screening should be essentially the same as for cisgender men, though there is no clear cut-off for PSA.31,35 Skin LGBTQ+ peoples may have higher rates of sun exposure, ultraviolet tanning and sunburn when compared with the general population,36 though this may not translate to clear increases in skin cancer.37–39 International studies are unlikely to be generalisable to the Australian population because of their retrospective nature and our cumulative sun exposure and skin cancer risk profiles.38,39 In the absence of further information, annual self-checks are recommended (noting they will miss lesions out of view), more frequently for higher-risk patients, with medical skin checks performed as needed on the basis of risk profile or discovery of concerning lesions.40 Skin cancer prevention advice should be universal, especially for those at higher risk.40,41 A skin check for TGD patients may potentially provoke dysphoria, especially if requiring full exposure for whole-body photography; clear discussion of the examination and consideration of modifications, such as limited exposure of the body part being examined at the time, would be recommended. LGBTQIA+-specific screening and surveillance Some tumours merit special discussion in regard to LGBTQIA+ populations, as follows. Meningioma and prolactinoma Meningioma is a rare, usually benign, tumour of the meninges12 associated with use of cyproterone acetate, a synthetic progestin, especially (though not exclusively42) higher cumulative doses over the lifespan – they may exert mass effects requiring treatment.12,34 Transgender women taking cyproterone have a four times higher incidence of meningioma when compared with cisgender women.34 Prolactinomas, which are similarly rare tumours,5 have also been reported at four times the rate in transgender women when compared with cisgender counterparts.34 Cyproterone34 and a number of other medications (including GAHT) and health conditions43 are known to cause hyperprolactinaemia.44 No specific screening for either tumour is recommended,5,44 though patients and clinicians should be alert to the small increased risk as well as signs and symptoms of concern, such as visual field changes and galactorrhoea, with further investigation and referral as appropriate. Genital tract cancers Given some gender affirming surgeries may include oophorectomy, hysterectomy and orchidectomy, consideration of cancers of these organs and related tissues, such as the endometrium, needs to be discussed on an individual basis. There is little evidence to screen for endometrial or uterine cancer,6 though symptoms such as abnormal uterine bleeding, discharge, pain and masses should be investigated,17 ideally supported by an affirmative gynaecologist.45 Menstruation typically ceases 3–6 months after beginning masculinising GAHT,46 but it can persist past 12 months.4 After ensuring adequate testosterone levels (10–15 nmol/L4; common reasons for ongoing menses include inadequate serum testosterone and topical administration methods47,48), investigation for abnormal uterine bleeding should proceed.45 Ovarian cancer risk in TGD peoples is not considered higher than in their cisgender counterparts,6 but investigation of symptoms should occur as for non-TGD peoples.17 Masculinising GAHT may cause endometrial hyperplasia; while in theory this would increase the risk of subsequent endometrial cancer, this has not been supported by clinical evidence to date.12 For TGD women following gender affirmative surgery, neovaginal cancer has been reported, with squamous cell carcinomas and adenocarcinomas, depending on tissue source (skin or gastrointestinal tract, respectively); some are associated with HPV.6 Screening, such as via self-examination, at routine intervals is recommended in the US.6 Routine testicular self-examination is recommended for people with testes, though the risk of cancer in transgender women is approximately similar to that in cisgender men.37 Supporting increased screening Higher screening rates are, at least in part, linked to higher rates of patient engagement. This depends on creating safer spaces for LGBTQIA+ individuals – both through inclusive environments and through practitioner training and confidence. Promotion of a safer environment may be by posters and signs; practice forms and paperwork; the practice website; visible iconography, such as flags; and inclusiveness training for practice staff, including reception and administrative staff.26 Training to improve cancer screening and prevention at a practice level for all communities is available,10 for example, via the Primary Care Cancer Control Quality Improvement Toolkit.8 Cervical screening engagement resources were mentioned above, which would also be suitable for practice nurses.26 Clinician- and patient-centred information can be found via sites such as TransHub (www.transhub.org.au) and through work with communities of practice, in person or online. Practice nurses may also be an untapped resource with significant potential for patient contact. Upskilling practice nurses to support cancer (and overall) screening and prevention, during management planning and via patient education, may be an effective and time-saving method to share the load in general practice while improving nurse autonomy and scope of practice.1,18 Conclusion Cancer screening and prevention is a key function of the general practitioner in primary care. In LGBTQIA+ populations, including TGD peoples, this largely follows the same recommendations as the non-LGBTQIA+ population, although an individualised approach is required, with some specific caveats based on which organs and tissues the individual possesses. Multiple barriers to screening exist; these need to be explored on a case-by-case basis and addressed, where possible, via clinical flexibility and appropriate modifications, including upskilling of other practice staff. Improving uptake of appropriate cancer screening and prevention activities by patient education and recommendation, and by incorporating it within management plans, will better support early detection and improved cancer outcomes for LGBTQIA+ peoples. content: Startups Tech Health Energy Impact More fighting cancer New statewide plan aims to eliminate cervical cancer in Texas by 2032 Laura Furr Mericas Oct 9, 2026, 8:30 am The five-year plan was launched during the CPRIT 2026 Innovations Conference in Galveston this month. Photo via Unsplash.com MD Anderson, on behalf of a coalition of health systems, has announced a new plan to eliminate cervical cancer in Texas. The five-year Texas Lone Star Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan was launched during the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT) 2026 Innovations Conference in Galveston this month. The plan focuses on three major pillars with goals to be achieved by 2032: HPV vaccination: Increase the percentage of Texas boys and girls up to date on human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination by age 15 from 50.5 percent to 80 percent Cervical cancer screening: Raise the share of Texas women up to date on cervical cancer screening from 64 percent to 80 percent Timely follow-up, diagnosis and treatment: Ensure 80 percent of women receive diagnostic follow-up and treatment when needed through community outreach, patient navigation, provider training and survivorship support Overall, the coalition wants to see fewer than four new cases of cervical cancer annually per 100,000 Texas women by 2032, according to a news release from MD Anderson. Currently, Texas has an incidence rate of 9.5 women per 100,000 diagnosed with cervical cancer, compared with 7.5 women per 100,000 nationally. “Texas has the tools to prevent nearly every case of cervical cancer, but tools can save lives only when people can utilize them,” Dr. Ernest Hawk, vice president and division head of Cancer Prevention and Population Sciences at MD Anderson, said in the release. “The Lone Star Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan gives us a shared roadmap to vaccinate more of our children, screen more of our women and make sure every abnormal result leads to care. With innovations like HPV self-collection and the commitment of partners across the state, elimination is within reach.” About 40 other hospitals, health care organizations and companies join MD Anderson in the coalition that launched the Lonestar Plan. Those based in Houston include Houston Methodist, Rice University, UTHealth Houston, Texas Children's Hospital, Houston Health Department and others. The CPRIT also announced its Texans Conquer Cancer Awards and its CPRIT Champion awards during the Innovations Conference this week. Several are based in Houston, including: Zhiqiang An, co-founder of CrossBridge Bio, Director of the Texas Therapeutics Institute, and Vice President of Drug Discovery at the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston Dr. Abbey Berenson, Director of the UTMB Center for Interdisciplinary Research in Women's Health Care Dr. Michael Taylor, Chair of Pediatric Neuro-Oncology at Texas Children's Cancer and Hematology Center and Director of Texas Children's Pediatric Brain Tumor Research Program To date, the CPRIT has awarded more than $4.2 billion in grants to fight cancer in the state. Over the summer, it awarded four $2 million grants to institutions in Houston and Bryan for the creation or expansion of “core” cancer research facilities. Texas Medical Center Innovation recently announced that its $2 million grant would renew its Accelerator for Cancer Therapeutics for five years. Read more from TMCi about the renewal here. content: FILE – A patient receives a vaccine protecting against human papillomavirus (HPV) at a pharmacy in Miami, Sept. 9, 2025. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell, File) By Associated Press PUBLISHED: October 7, 2026 at 10:10 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... By MIKE STOBBE, AP Medical Writer NEW YORK (AP) — Preteens may soon have something to celebrate: Medical experts are discussing the possibility that one dose of a life-saving cancer vaccine, instead of two, may be enough to protect them. U.S. vaccination recommendations have become splintered in the past year, with federal officials and doctors’ organizations disagreeing over guidance and even battling each other in court. But both sides have been exploring revisions in longstanding HPV vaccine recommendations. “This would be a significant shift in terms of what has been communicated for many years about the best way to protect adolescents against HPV,” said Jason Schwartz, a Yale University vaccine policy researcher. Here’s a look at HPV shots, which debuted 20 years ago and may now be approaching a crossroads. HPV is linked to thousands of cancer cases HPV, human papillomavirus, is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the U.S. More than 40 HPV types can infect the genital areas of men and women, plus the lining of the mouth and throat. Certain strains are responsible for most cases of genital warts. HPV also is a leading cause of the nearly 50,000 cancer cases diagnosed in the U.S. each year that affect those parts of the body. Indeed, about 90% of cervical cancer and anal cancers are attributed to HPV infections , according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In 2006, federal health officials approved the first HPV vaccine, Merck & Co.’s Gardasil. A second vaccine was approved in 2009, GlaxoSmithKline’s Cervarix. Both vaccines are approved for use in males and females, available for kids as young as 9 to adults in their 20s. But they were prioritized for 11- and 12-year-olds, because the shots work best if given before someone is sexually active. HPV vaccination recommendations have changed before Initially, in 2006, HPV vaccinations were recommended only for girls and given as a series of three shots over six months. Boys were added in 2011, a move largely intended to stop them from spreading a virus to girls that could cause cervical cancer. Ten years ago, the government changed the dosing recommendations. It dropped the number of recommended doses from three to two after studies showed that amount offered sufficient protection. Research also suggested two doses worked better when spaced six to 12 months apart, meaning they could be given at annual checkups. Since then, studies in multiple countries have shown dramatic decreases in infections, genital warts cases and precancerous cervical lesions. In 2020, the American Cancer Society updated its guidelines for women, raising the age at which screenings should start to 25, from 21. The organization attributed the change to data indicating vaccinations had led to a drop in rates of cervical changes that are seen as precursors to cancer. Evidence has continued to be favorable. The University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project this year published a research review that found that HPV vaccines had lowered the risk of genital-area cancers in women. And a study published in April in the journal JAMA Oncology found vaccinated males are nearly 50% less likely to develop cancers of the head and neck, esophagus, anus or penis. What’s more, “the duration of protection is long,” said Angela Ulrich, who led the Vaccine Integrity Project review. “We have people who are 20, 30, 40 years old who are seeing protection from the HPV vaccine.” HPV vaccination rates are lower than for other vaccines A recent CDC report found vaccination rates against HPV were lower than the rates for some other shots adolescents get, at least partly because most states don’t require HPV vaccinations as a condition of school attendance. Still, the HPV vaccination rate has been flat for four years in a row, with about 63% of teenagers getting both doses. It doesn’t help that HPV shots are known to have a sharper sting. (Doctors have noted fainting is more common after HPV shots.) Questions about pain are common, said Dr. Scott Hadland, who works at a Boston clinic that treats adolescents and young adults. “Some of my patients tell me it hurts more than other vaccines they’ve received, but only for a moment,” he said. Also not helping lately, perhaps, is the elevation of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to U.S. health secretary. Before he was appointed to oversee federal health agencies last year, Kennedy was an attorney and consultant in lawsuits against Merck over the Gardasil vaccine, and falsely claimed the vaccine increases cervical cancer risk. Research suggests one shot may be enough for girls In January, Kennedy ordered the number of recommended HPV doses to be reduced to one, as part of a unilateral reduction of the childhood vaccination schedule. That change was blocked by a federal judge’s order, but it actually is something that medical experts had been considering for some time. The idea gained attention late last year with the publication of a study in Costa Rica that tracked more than 20,000 girls over five years. It found a single HPV shot provided about 97% protection against cervical cancer, similar to two doses. A year earlier, in 2024, research developments prompted a CDC advisory committee to form a work group to explore the possibility of a revised recommendation. That work was interrupted when Kennedy dismissed the members of the committee. The American Academy of Pediatrics — one of the medical groups that sued Kennedy — makes its own vaccination recommendations. It has been considering a guidance change, exploring questions such as whether one dose is sufficient for at least some people and at what age vaccination should begin, said Dr. James Campbell, chair of the organization’s committee on infectious diseases. Should kids get one shot or two? Recommendations are evolving. But right now, experts advise that kids get two shots. While there is evidence showing one shot was sufficient for girls in preventing cervical cancer, there is less evidence about other kinds of cancer in girls. Also lacking is data on whether one shot is sufficient protection for boys against the HPV-related cancers they are at risk for, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project review. Whether the recommendation remains two shots or is changed to one, it’s important that kids get vaccinated, Hadland said. “The benefits are very clear. It prevents cancer,” he said. By MIKE STOBBE, AP Medical Writer NEW YORK (AP) — Preteens may soon have something to celebrate: Medical experts are discussing the possibility that one dose of a life-saving cancer vaccine, instead of two, may be enough to protect them. U.S. vaccination recommendations have become splintered in the past year, with federal officials and doctors’ organizations disagreeing over guidance and even battling each other in court. But both sides have been exploring revisions in longstanding HPV vaccine recommendations. “This would be a significant shift in terms of what has been communicated for many years about the best way to protect adolescents against HPV,” said Jason Schwartz, a Yale University vaccine policy researcher. Here’s a look at HPV shots, which debuted 20 years ago and may now be approaching a crossroads. HPV is linked to thousands of cancer cases HPV, human papillomavirus, is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the U.S. More than 40 HPV types can infect the genital areas of men and women, plus the lining of the mouth and throat. Certain strains are responsible for most cases of genital warts. HPV also is a leading cause of the nearly 50,000 cancer cases diagnosed in the U.S. each year that affect those parts of the body. Indeed, about 90% of cervical cancer and anal cancers are attributed to HPV infections, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In 2006, federal health officials approved the first HPV vaccine, Merck & Co.’s Gardasil. A second vaccine was approved in 2009, GlaxoSmithKline’s Cervarix. Both vaccines are approved for use in males and females, available for kids as young as 9 to adults in their 20s. But they were prioritized for 11- and 12-year-olds, because the shots work best if given before someone is sexually active. HPV vaccination recommendations have changed before Initially, in 2006, HPV vaccinations were recommended only for girls and given as a series of three shots over six months. Boys were added in 2011, a move largely intended to stop them from spreading a virus to girls that could cause cervical cancer. Ten years ago, the government changed the dosing recommendations. It dropped the number of recommended doses from three to two after studies showed that amount offered sufficient protection. Research also suggested two doses worked better when spaced six to 12 months apart, meaning they could be given at annual checkups. Since then, studies in multiple countries have shown dramatic decreases in infections, genital warts cases and precancerous cervical lesions. In 2020, the American Cancer Society updated its guidelines for women, raising the age at which screenings should start to 25, from 21. The organization attributed the change to data indicating vaccinations had led to a drop in rates of cervical changes that are seen as precursors to cancer. Evidence has continued to be favorable. The University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project this year published a research review that found that HPV vaccines had lowered the risk of genital-area cancers in women. And a study published in April in the journal JAMA Oncology found vaccinated males are nearly 50% less likely to develop cancers of the head and neck, esophagus, anus or penis. What’s more, “the duration of protection is long,” said Angela Ulrich, who led the Vaccine Integrity Project review. “We have people who are 20, 30, 40 years old who are seeing protection from the HPV vaccine.” HPV vaccination rates are lower than for other vaccines A recent CDC report found vaccination rates against HPV were lower than the rates for some other shots adolescents get, at least partly because most states don’t require HPV vaccinations as a condition of school attendance. Still, the HPV vaccination rate has been flat for four years in a row, with about 63% of teenagers getting both doses. It doesn’t help that HPV shots are known to have a sharper sting. (Doctors have noted fainting is more common after HPV shots.) Questions about pain are common, said Dr. Scott Hadland, who works at a Boston clinic that treats adolescents and young adults. “Some of my patients tell me it hurts more than other vaccines they’ve received, but only for a moment,” he said. Also not helping lately, perhaps, is the elevation of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to U.S. health secretary. Before he was appointed to oversee federal health agencies last year, Kennedy was an attorney and consultant in lawsuits against Merck over the Gardasil vaccine, and falsely claimed the vaccine increases cervical cancer risk. Research suggests one shot may be enough for girls In January, Kennedy ordered the number of recommended HPV doses to be reduced to one, as part of a unilateral reduction of the childhood vaccination schedule. That change was blocked by a federal judge’s order, but it actually is something that medical experts had been considering for some time. The idea gained attention late last year with the publication of a study in Costa Rica that tracked more than 20,000 girls over five years. It found a single HPV shot provided about 97% protection against cervical cancer, similar to two doses. A year earlier, in 2024, research developments prompted a CDC advisory committee to form a work group to explore the possibility of a revised recommendation. That work was interrupted when Kennedy dismissed the members of the committee. The American Academy of Pediatrics — one of the medical groups that sued Kennedy — makes its own vaccination recommendations. It has been considering a guidance change, exploring questions such as whether one dose is sufficient for at least some people and at what age vaccination should begin, said Dr. James Campbell, chair of the organization’s committee on infectious diseases. Should kids get one shot or two? Recommendations are evolving. But right now, experts advise that kids get two shots. While there is evidence showing one shot was sufficient for girls in preventing cervical cancer, there is less evidence about other kinds of cancer in girls. Also lacking is data on whether one shot is sufficient protection for boys against the HPV-related cancers they are at risk for, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project review. Whether the recommendation remains two shots or is changed to one, it’s important that kids get vaccinated, Hadland said. “The benefits are very clear. It prevents cancer,” he said. content: Reduction in HPV vaccine uptake ‘worrying’, Director of Public Health says The reduction in uptake of the HPV vaccine is “worrying”, the Director of Public Health Dr Helen Carter has said, pointing that uptake is aimed at 90% under World Health Organisation guidelines. By contrast the uptake in Gibraltar last year was 63%. The HPV (Human Papillomavirus) vaccine prevents cervical cancer in women and genital cancers in men, and in countries where the vaccine had been administered earlier than in Gibraltar, like Australia where they are seeing “almost no” cases of cervical cancer in the age groups which have been vaccinated. Dr Carter said the number of students being vaccinated for HPV was reducing annually and encouraged parents to consider uptake even if they had missed the vaccine previously. The HPV vaccine is offered to boys and girls in school Year 8, aged approximately 12 to 13 years, and those who are older can still take up the vaccine. Dr Carter said the HPV used to be offered in three doses and is now in one vaccine, and encouraged parents to give consent to prevent cancer. “I would love to see cervical cancer eliminated in my lifetime,” she said. The vaccination programme began on October 2 in Gibraltar’s comprehensive schools, with Health Visitors attending Westside and Bayside Schools to commence vaccinations. HPV is a very common virus and while most HPV infections cause no symptoms and clear naturally, some types can cause cancers, including cancers of the cervix, anus, genital areas and head and neck, as well as genital warts. Vaccinating at an early age is most effective as this provides protection before young people are likely to come into contact with the virus. The HPV vaccine prevents cervical cancer because it targets the high-risk HPV strains responsible for the majority of cervical cancer cases. This makes HPV vaccination an important opportunity to protect future generations and work towards the elimination of cervical cancer altogether. The HPV vaccine has been used worldwide for many years and has a strong safety record. The impact of HPV vaccination has been demonstrated in countries with high vaccination uptake. In some countries the number of genital wart diagnoses among young people fell by more than 90% following the introduction of the national HPV vaccination programme. Members of the public under 25 years old who have missed their HPV vaccination when previously eligible may still be able to receive the vaccination, subject to the applicable eligibility criteria. Anyone who has missed their vaccination during the school vaccination programme is encouraged to call 20003351 or contact the CHC on 20007962 to book an appointment. For further information about the HPV vaccine, including eligibility, benefits and possible side effects, please visit the Gibraltar Health Authority – HPV Vaccine information page

content: No, You Won't Catch HPV From a Train Seat Doctors say the viral chart is misleading. Here's what is on the seat, and what helps. A chart has been going around online. It puts high-speed rail seats near the top of a table of HPV sources. Hotel toilet seats, armrests, and tray tables show up too. The chart has arrows, percentages, and a warning tone. That format makes it look like evidence. The science underneath is thin. The first problem is what a positive surface test means. Many of these charts lean on studies that used PCR to detect HPV DNA. PCR is sensitive. It can find a fragment of viral DNA. A fragment is not a whole virus. A whole virus is not always infectious. To infect someone, a virus has to be intact and able to enter a cell and copy itself. A positive swab on a seat can mean a DNA trace is there. It does not mean a live, infectious virus is waiting. Think of a fire that has burned out. Ash can still hold chemical traces of what burned. The ash cannot start the next fire. A PCR-positive surface is closer to that ash than to a live flame. Li Tongzeng is chief physician in the Department of Infectious Diseases at Beijing Youan Hospital, Capital Medical University. He said the chart is unreliable and the public does not need to panic. HPV is fragile outside the body, he said. It survives poorly on dry surfaces. On fabric or hard plastic, such as a train seat, it is very unlikely to stay intact and infectious. HPV spreads mainly through sexual contact or close, direct skin-to-skin contact. Indirect transmission through public objects is extremely low, almost negligible. What HPV is and how it spreads HPV is a small DNA virus. More than 200 types have been identified. They fall into two broad groups. Skin types infect the skin. They cause common warts, plantar warts, and flat warts. These can spread through skin contact, often when there is a small break in the skin. Mucosal types infect mucous membranes. Low-risk types can cause genital warts. High-risk types are linked to cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV does not travel through the blood. It infects epithelial cells. For mucosal HPV to reach a train seat, a person would have to leave virus from genital, anal, or oral mucosa on the seat. Clothing blocks the genital and anal route. Spitting on a seat is not normal behavior. That leaves skin HPV as the only plausible source on a seat. Skin HPV can shed from a wart. Even then, the next passenger would need several things at once: enough active virus, a break in the skin, and prolonged rubbing or friction at the contact point. Sitting down for a moment does not meet those conditions. A quick brush against a seat does not meet them either. No official public health agency has reported a case of HPV infection linked to a public seat. What is on the seat This does not mean train seats are sterile. They are public surfaces. They can carry bacteria, fungi, and skin scales. A passenger with athlete's foot who takes off their shoes and steps on the seat can leave fungal scales behind. A passenger who puts feet on a tray table can leave dirt and skin cells there. These are reasons for basic hygiene. They are not reasons to fear HPV. Wang Chun is associate chief physician in the Department of Dermatology at Southwest Hospital, Army Medical University. Wang noted that the risk from indirect contact depends on the person. People with weaker immunity, diabetes, or other underlying conditions may be more likely to pick up bacteria or fungi from public objects. People with broken skin, recent shaving or friction wounds, or heavy sweating during long, hot rides may also face a slightly higher exposure risk. For them, physical barriers and hand hygiene can lower the chance of an accidental exposure. Do disposable seat covers help? For HPV, no. Li Tongzeng said alcohol wipes and disposable seat covers mainly provide psychological comfort. They may help against ordinary bacteria and fungi. They do very little to reduce HPV risk. A seat cover can block grease, dust, and some skin scales. If it makes a long trip feel cleaner, use one. Do not treat it as armor against HPV. The virus does not spread through a dry seat surface in the way the chart suggests. What works Get the HPV vaccine. It lowers the risk of high-risk HPV infection and precancerous changes. Wash your hands. Do it after touching handrails, seat belts, and tray tables. Do it before eating. Do not touch your mouth, nose, or eyes with unwashed hands. Cover cuts. If you have a fresh wound, put a bandage or sterile gauze over it. That keeps bacteria and fungi in the environment away from broken skin. Wear long pants or a long skirt if your skin is sensitive. It creates a simple physical barrier between you and the seat. Do not put your feet on the tray table or the back of the seat in front of you. Do not take off your shoes and stand or sit on the seat. Those habits leave skin scales, dirt, and fungi for the next passenger. They also make the ride worse for everyone around you. The cleaning standard Railway 12306 customer service has said that high-speed rail seat cushions are removed and sent for deep cleaning every 120 to 180 days. In sleeper cars, bedding is changed for each passenger. The railway says these practices meet its sanitation and disease-control standards. A train seat is not sterile. It is a public surface with a cleaning schedule. That schedule is not the same as an HPV hotspot. What to do The claim that high-speed rail seats are a leading source of HPV does not hold. A positive PCR result on a surface can be a DNA trace. It is not proof of a live, infectious virus. HPV spreads through sexual contact or close skin-to-skin contact. A dry seat is a poor route for it. Use a seat cover if it makes you comfortable. Wash your hands. Cover a cut. Get vaccinated. Keep your feet off the tray table and the seat. Those steps address the risks that are present. The HPV hotspot label is not one of them. About the Creator Jin Writer of reamstories https://reamstories.com/jin Enjoyed the story? The findings provide important new evidence as countries work toward the World Health Organization’s goal of eliminating cervical cancer. Women living with HIV are six times more likely to be infected with HPV and twice as likely to die from invasive cervical cancer than those without HIV, making vaccination particularly important for this population. Published in The Lancet HIV, the study followed women living with HIV for up to nine years after HPV vaccination — the longest study to date examining how well the vaccine works in this population. Until now, researchers had little evidence about the vaccine’s effectiveness in women living with HIV beyond two years. Dr. Elisabeth McClymont “We’ve known for some time that HPV vaccines are safe and highly effective, but we didn’t have long-term evidence to show how lasting that protection is for women living with HIV,” said first author Dr. Elisabeth McClymont, assistant professor in the UBC Faculty of Medicine’s department of obstetrics and gynaecology and department of pediatrics. “Our findings are incredibly reassuring. Even in a population whose immune systems can be affected by HIV, vaccination provided strong protection against HPV infection and cervical cancer for many years.” The study included 293 women living with HIV in Canada and was conducted through 14 HIV and gynecological care clinics across the country. The researchers found that the vaccine produced a strong immune response that was sustained over time. Among women who received all three doses and did not already have the strains of HPV targeted by the vaccine, rates of HPV infection and genital warts were very low, and no participants developed serious precancerous changes to the cervix caused by those HPV strains. The researchers also found that maintaining an undetectable HIV viral load was important for sustaining HPV antibody levels over time, underscoring the importance of continued access to HIV treatment and care. Dr. Deborah Money The findings could have particular significance globally. Nearly 20 million women and girls are living with HIV worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in sub-Saharan Africa, where access to cervical cancer screening can also be limited. “Cervical cancer is preventable, yet it continues to take lives in Canada and around the world, particularly in places where HIV rates are higher and access to screening and prevention is limited,” said senior author Dr. Deborah Money, professor and head of the UBC Faculty of Medicine’s department of obstetrics and gynaecology. “We now have concrete evidence that HPV vaccination works very well for women living with HIV over the long term. Making this vaccine more accessible and acceptable for those who need it most can help us prevent unnecessary deaths and move closer to eliminating cervical cancer globally.” This study was supported by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the CIHR Canadian HIV Trials Network, and an in-kind contribution from Merck Canada. content_title: Kovina Therapeutics Awarded $2.3 Million NCI Grant To Advance HPV Cancer Therapy
content: Kovina Therapeutics has received a $2.3 million Direct-to-Phase II Small Business Innovation Research award from the National Cancer Institute to advance its lead oral small-molecule therapy targeting HPV-driven cancers. The two-year award will support Investigational New Drug-enabling development of Kovina’s lead program. Kovina is developing first-in-class small molecules designed to directly target the Human Papillomavirus E6 oncoprotein. E6 contributes to HPV-positive cancers by degrading the tumor suppressor p53 and is required for HPV-positive cancer cell survival. Kovina’s approach is intended to inhibit E6 and restore p53 function. The award follows publication of Kovina research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that validated direct pharmacologic targeting of HPV E6. The research demonstrated restoration of p53 tumor suppressor activity, selective killing of HPV-positive cancer cells and tumor growth inhibition in HPV-positive preclinical models. The NCI funding will support chemistry, manufacturing and controls work, IND-enabling pharmacology and toxicology and other activities required to prepare an IND application. Kovina noted that HPV causes an estimated 39,300 cancers annually in the U.S. despite the availability of preventive vaccines. The company believes direct targeting of E6 could ultimately have applications across HPV-associated disease ranging from premalignant conditions to invasive cancers. KEY QUOTES: “This award comes at an important point for Kovina as we move from compelling preclinical science into formal development. Together with our recent PNAS publication, the NCI support gives us significant momentum as we advance our lead program through IND-enabling development and toward the clinic.” Kristin Sherman, Chief Executive Officer of Kovina Therapeutics “HPV E6 has long been recognized as a compelling cancer target but directly inhibiting it with a small molecule has been challenging. Our work demonstrates that E6 can be specifically targeted, restoring p53 and selectively killing HPV-positive cancer cells. This gives us a strong foundation for translating the biology into a new therapeutic approach.” Elliot Androphy, M.D., Founder and Chief Scientific Officer of Kovina Therapeutics Thank you for visiting Pulse 2.0. A statement from the GHA follows below: The Gibraltar Health Authority will begin its HPV vaccination programme in Gibraltar’s comprehensive schools on Friday 2 October 2026, with Health Visitors attending Westside and Bayside Schools to commence vaccinations. The HPV vaccine is being offered to boys and girls in School Year 8, aged approximately 12–13 years. HPV (Human Papillomavirus) is a very common virus. While most HPV infections cause no symptoms and clear naturally, some types can cause cancers, including cancers of the cervix, anus, genital areas and head and neck, as well as genital warts. HPV vaccination is not just for girls. Boys can also be affected by HPV and can develop HPV-related cancers. Vaccinating at an early age is most effective as this provides protection before young people are likely to come into contact with the virus. The HPV vaccine prevents cervical cancer because it targets the high-risk HPV strains responsible for the majority of cervical cancer cases. This makes HPV vaccination an important opportunity to protect future generations and work towards the elimination of cervical cancer altogether. The HPV vaccine has been used worldwide for many years and has a strong safety record. The impact of HPV vaccination has been demonstrated in countries with high vaccination uptake. In some countries the number of genital wart diagnoses among young people fell by more than 90% following the introduction of the national HPV vaccination programme. Members of the public under 25 years old who have missed their HPV vaccination when previously eligible may still be able to receive the vaccination, subject to the applicable eligibility criteria. Anyone who has missed their vaccination during the school vaccination programme is encouraged to call 20003351 or contact the CHC on 20007962 to book an appointment.
